s15.slug: FRIDAY · 4:35 PM · THE LIGHTHOUSE, THE BACK PORCH
body: The sun is ten minutes off the Channel and going down into it orange, and the Lighthouse’s back porch has turned the color of a peach crate. A laptop in the kitchen window is playing something slow that sounds recorded underwater. The surfers who rent the place have a keg in a trash can of ice by the steps, FRIDAY THE 13TH on the lid in Sharpie and a horseshoe hung on the tap.

Theo got back from La Cañada at three and stood in the doorway of 412 in the blazer until Jack got up. “Come drink something with a label, Costigan.” Now he’s leaning on a porch post with a Stella, and Jack is working the porch.

He has three surfers with their wetsuits peeled to the waist and a girl in a Marisol Crew sweatshirt, and he’s giving them Friday the thirteenth as a feast of the Church: Philip the Fair arrested every Templar in France on a Friday the thirteenth, 1307 — so it’s a solemnity in Paris and a holy day of obligation for anybody with a castle. The keg, he tells them, is a sacramental. Not a sacrament — it can’t confer grace on its own; it depends entirely on the disposition of the recipient — and he blesses it with a red Solo cup, and they cheer. Then Youngstown’s eleven seasons, on his fingers: winter, fake spring, real winter, Lent, pothole, construction, summer (a Tuesday), Browns hope, Browns despair, deer, and Christmas. The surfers love Youngstown. One of them wants to go.
Theo, from the post, not loud: “That’s three bits in a row. You don’t do three.”

Jack does a fourth. The surfer with the St. Christopher on a bootlace, it turns out, is wearing a saint the Vatican took off the calendar in 1969. That makes him the only man on this porch surfing uninsured. The porch laughs. Theo looks at Jack over the neck of the Stella, and lets him have it, and takes the Stella into the house.

When the laugh is done Jack is looking west, past the end of the rail and the gap in the back fence, out to the Point. The light out there has gone the color of weak tea. The dead lighthouse stands up black against it, and below it, small, at the low stone wall by the white cross, a man sits with a guitar case open on the stones beside him. Jack knows the set of the shoulders from a stool at Bastille. Julian is playing to nobody, and the wind brings none of it this far.

The screen door bangs. Theo comes out with two Coronas, a lime wedged in each neck, and stops beside him at the rail and sees where Jack is looking. He puts one of the bottles in Jack’s hand. Then he goes back inside, and he does not look west.

The bottle is so cold it aches in his palm. Jack holds it until the sun is gone, and then he sets it on the rail, full, the lime floating, and walks home across the Grove with the eucalyptus black overhead and his hands in the pockets of the Carhartt.

By ten the fourth-floor lounge has been annexed by organic chemistry. Three Bio 1A pre-meds have the big table under a drift of Priya’s old flashcards, laminated in 2007 and handed down like a family Bible, and Kevin stands at the whiteboard in a gray quarter-zip, drawing an enolate for the fourth time. Doug is asleep on the couch under a fleece blanket with a wizard on it. Jack has the other end of the couch and Hale’s reader open on his knee and hasn’t read a line of it in an hour.

He’s been doing the reagents. LDA is St. Jerome: bulky, bad-tempered, won’t attack anybody, just walks in and takes the least-crowded proton out of spite. Grignards are Jesuits — brilliant, they’ll react with absolutely anything, and one drop of water ruins them. The pre-meds have been writing it on Priya’s flashcards in Sharpie. One of them, a sunburned kid from Visalia named Garrett, has laughed loudest at every one of them and slapped the table.

It’s Garrett who brings up Maine. He says it capping a highlighter, conversational, as if it were the weather. “Honestly, Maine got it right. It’s just biology. Marriage is a reproductive unit.” The girl beside him nods at her flashcard.

Kevin caps the marker and turns around. “Biology doesn’t vote, Garrett,” he says, each word set down separately, like instruments on a tray. “People do.” He puts the marker on the ledge. “And you’d fail Bio 1A on that definition.”
The table goes quiet. Garrett laughs once, waiting for the rest of the joke, and there isn’t any rest.

Then Kevin’s smile comes back, all its team-captain wattage, half a second late and on crooked, like a picture hung in a hurry. “Getting water,” he says. “Carbonyls. Don’t touch my enolate.” The lounge door swings behind him. Through the wall Jack hears the stairwell door, and Kevin’s feet on the stairs going up, not down.

choices.key: Friday night Kevin walked out of the orgo group. You followed him into the stairwell.
response: Jack leaves Hale open on the arm of the couch and goes out after him.

Jack turns the room. It isn’t hard. He does Garrett as a Grignard reagent — eager, reacts with everything, undone by the first drop of water — until Garrett is laughing at himself, red to the ears, and by twenty to eleven he has the table back on carbonyls, St. Jerome and all. Kevin’s chair stays pushed out from the table, the marker on the ledge where he left it.

journal.title: Kevin Tran
journal.text: Kevin Tran. Goes to daily Mass, saves you a seat with a Bible. Has a sister, Tina, in dental school, who flossed in the womb. Lies to his mom about orgo in Vietnamese. Drives his mother’s Odyssey at sixty-five, not sixty-six. His dad has two nail-salon supply stores in San Jose and has never had a Labor Day. Brought six pairs of gloves to a beach cleanup. Mouthed every word of Joey’s first reading from the second pew. Somebody coached Joey; I can guess who. Brought tea to a wake. His Bà Nội says heaven makes the elephant and heaven makes the grass. Walked Margot down at four in the morning. Handed Lena a roll of quarters for the payphone before she asked. Halloween: All Saints, every one nobody’s heard of — scrubs, a halo and a white mask. He found Laney. Friday night a pre-med said Maine got it right. Kevin said one sentence to him and went to get water.

s16a.slug: FRIDAY · 10:22 PM · DELGADO HALL, EAST STAIRWELL, BETWEEN FOUR AND FIVE
body: The east stairwell is painted cinderblock and caged bulbs and ten degrees colder than the hall. Jack is halfway up the flight between four and five when he hears them, a landing above, at the top, where the roof door says ALARM WILL SOUND and doesn’t mean it.
Kevin’s voice, low and fast, nothing sunny in it. “You said you’d never —”
And Theo’s, lower. “I haven’t.”

Jack’s sneaker squeaks on the tread. Above him both of them look down over the rail: Kevin with one hand on the push bar of the roof door; Theo on the top step with his knees up and his iPhone dark in his hands.
“Costigan!” Theo says, in his dinner-party voice. “We were discussing Doug’s sleepwalking.”

Kevin comes down the stairs. On the way past he puts a hand on Jack’s shoulder for one step — warm through the flannel, there and gone — and goes on down to four, to the lounge and the enolate and Garrett.
Theo doesn’t get up. He turns the dark phone over and over between his knees and waits, perfectly friendly, for Jack to go back down.

s16b.slug: FRIDAY · 11:05 PM · DELGADO HALL, EAST STAIRWELL, 4TH-FLOOR LANDING
body: At five past eleven Jack sits on the third step up from the fourth-floor landing, where the one bar lives, and calls Glenwood Avenue.

It rings in the kitchen in Youngstown, where it’s after two in the morning — six times, eight — and goes to the machine: his mother’s voice, recorded the year Rosie was born, asking him to leave a message for the Costigans, God bless. He hangs up before the beep. The house is asleep. There’s no one at the table with a rosary, waiting on a truck. He sits there with the phone shut in his hand and lets himself have that.
From above him, up past five, by the roof door, Kevin’s voice comes down the stairwell, low and fast. “You said you’d never —”
And Theo’s, lower. “I haven’t.”
Somebody opens the roof door on the night and lets it shut again. The alarm doesn’t sound; it never has. Jack looks up the well of the stairs at the caged bulb on five, and doesn’t go up.

body.text: Then the Brick, the night desk, midnight to six.

body: On the lounge TV it’s the fourth quarter in Columbus under a sky the color of dishwater, the Horseshoe full to the rim and breathing steam, and in the lounge the blinds are half down against a California afternoon that doesn’t know what month it is.

Becca is on the carpet in front of the set, cross-legged, in his gray Cardinal Mooney hoodie with the sleeves rolled three times, explaining downs to a room that didn’t ask. Theo is on the arm of the couch with a Pellegrino. Laney has her bare feet on the coffee table, ankles crossed. Margot is in the armchair with a library Bourdieu open on her knee; she is here, she has said, to observe a ritual. Down the hall Kevin’s door has been shut since last night.

body.text: Jack has slept four hours since the night desk, from half past six to half past ten, and he has never been funnier.

body: Jack is calling the game from the couch, play by play. Pryor keeps it on third and long and goes left, all legs, six foot six of Jeannette, P-A — “the only man in Ohio who runs like he’s late for Mass.” Tressel on the sideline in the sweater vest: “That vest has been to more funeral luncheons than my nonna. That vest has opinions about the ham.” And his father’s theory, delivered as settled doctrine: the forward pass is a Protestant innovation, legal since 1906, and Notre Dame only went and perfected it to save it from them. Becca laughs at all of it with her head back against his shin, and corrects him on the downs.

At the TV timeout she gets up on her knees and pulls a flat package out from under the couch, where she has apparently been hiding it since before he got here. It’s wrapped in a Walgreens bag slit open and turned inside out, taped at every seam. “Okay,” she says. “Open it.”

body.text: It’s the two of them at Piedras Blancas at sunset, printed at the Walgreens on Mission, Kevin’s thumb a pink blur in one corner and the elephant seals heaped on the sand behind them like a delivery of sofas.
body.else: It’s the two of them on the bleachers at the Friday-night game, printed at the Walgreens on Mission, Kevin’s thumb a pink blur in one corner.

body: The frame is from the Goodwill, and she has painted it herself: elephant seals all the way around the border, gray and fat and very carefully done, and under each one, in tiny white capitals, what it weighs. 4,500 LBS. 1,600 LBS. 75 LBS (A PUP).
“For your desk,” Becca says. “Theo says you have no personal effects.”
“I said *affect*,” says Theo, from the arm of the couch.

Becca has plans. Gerald the turkey is thriving, which is the problem: her little brothers have taught him to come when he’s called, and her father says that’s the last thing a turkey ought to know. On Thanksgiving she’s going to call Jack at two o’clock her time, five in Ohio, during her dad’s grace — “so you can hear it. It’s eleven minutes. He does every cow.” She squeezes his arm and leaves the rest of Thanksgiving alone. “And next Saturday — The Game. Michigan. I looked it up.” It’s in her planner already, in green. “Can we watch it here? With you?”
Jack says they can watch it here.
Ohio State punts. Becca watches the ball go up and turn over at the top, and says, without looking away from it, “Someday I want to see your house. Is that okay to say?”
Jack tells her it’s okay to say.

Iowa ties it with a freshman quarterback named Vandenberg who wasn’t supposed to be playing, and the game goes to overtime, and in overtime Iowa comes up empty. Then Tressel sends out Devin Barclay, a walk-on who used to play pro soccer, to kick a thirty-nine-yarder for the Rose Bowl. Becca gets up on her knees with her hands together and prays a Glory Be out loud at the TV. Laney, who has a line for everything, says, “Amen.”
The ball goes through. Twenty-seven, twenty-four. Becca throws both arms up and hollers, and Theo applauds the television, and the announcers say *Pasadena* twice.

Margot turns a page. “That’s surface acting,” she says, not looking up. “Hochschild. *The Managed Heart*, 1983. Delta flight attendants, smiling through turbulence because the smile is the job.” She cites it like a bus schedule. “You’ve been doing it since yesterday. I was at the vending machine last night while you made three pre-meds laugh at carbonyls. Carbonyls aren’t funny, Costigan. I’ve checked.”
“He’s not acting,” Becca says. “He’s *happy*. They’re *winning*.”
Theo is already on his feet, pitching to the room at volume: “Terrelle Pryor. A small town in Pennsylvania. A mother who believed. Denzel as the coach — no. Denzel as the *vest*.”
Laney says nothing at all.

response: Jack stands up with the frame against his heart. “I’d like to thank the Academy. And my father, who taught me the forward pass is Protestant. And Jim Tressel’s vest, which couldn’t be here tonight.” The lounge laughs; Becca claps with the Walgreens bag in her lap. Margot looks at him over the Bourdieu for a second, turns the page, and writes nothing down.
On her way out Laney stops behind the couch and squeezes the back of his neck, once, hard, like a big sister, and goes down the hall without a word.
“Becca,” Jack says. “Explain downs to Margot.”

Becca turns round on the carpet to face the armchair and does, from first principles, with the coffee table for a field and Theo’s Pellegrino for the line to gain. Four tries to go ten yards; if you don’t, the other team gets it; you punt so they have farther to go. Margot closes the Bourdieu on her finger and listens to every word of it, to the end of fourth down.
On her way out Laney stops behind the couch and squeezes the back of his neck, once, hard, like a big sister, and goes down the hall without a word.
“Leave it, Margot.”
She looks at him over the book, and leaves it. Becca, folding the Walgreens bag into a neat square to keep, doesn’t notice anything.
On her way out Laney stops behind the couch and squeezes the back of his neck, once, hard, like a big sister, and goes down the hall without a word.

journal.title: Becca Lindell
journal.text: Coeur d’Alene. Seven siblings; wants seven or nine kids, odd numbers, for the tiebreaker. Can butcher a deer — elk too. Has pulled a calf, and it shows. Ran the beach cleanup like a cattle drive and put me on her team. Asked about the scar in the water. Told her mother the cleanup was a date, then asked me if it was. Wrote FRIDAY? on her clipboard, and meant it. Drives her brother Eli’s red Ranger; St. Isidore on the visor. Second date: Friday-night football. Knows downs. Prayed a Glory Be on fourth and one. Learned the First Way on the bleachers and said it back perfectly. Kissed my cheek so there’s no confusion. Third date was mine. I asked. I paid. The elephant seals at Piedras Blancas at sunset, in Kevin’s Odyssey. She knew what every one of them weighed. Nobody’s ever planned a thing for her, she says. She’s been praying for two in the morning. Named a hermit crab Thomas, after the First Way, and asked Fr. Osei whose blessing it was. Works the Marine Lab touch tank Thursday afternoons and Friday at six in the morning — that’s how she signed Thomas out. He’s home; she knows him by the chip in his shell. Mailed Rosie a birthday card with Thomas on it and six true facts on the back, to the address I gave her for her Christmas cards. She does them in October. Has a page on her clipboard for Wes. She’s been praying for him and Lena since September. Her eyes are gray. Brought a survival bag to the library for my midterm, with a clementine for Lena. Prays at two, like always. Took me to *Where the Wild Things Are* at the Rialto; her favorite line is the last one. My mother wrote her a thank-you note. Her list for Halloween says WE SHOULD MATCH!! It’s due Halloween. She says I look at her like homework. She says she’ll wait. Stuck on the touch tank all weekend while we were at Big Sur: the weekend volunteer has the swine flu. Asked me for the monks’ fruitcake for her Grandma Agnes — the only honest fruitcake in America. I handed in my homework six days early. St. Isidore and St. Maria: her first. Early, she said. Nobody’s early but her. Halloween: she sewed my costume out of a Rathdrum Feed & Seed sack. She was St. Maria de la Cabeza in Mrs. Fitch’s lace, with a water jug. Best Saint, by acclamation — a gold halo. Never won anything that wasn’t a heifer. Home at 11:40 for the six o’clock tank; the volunteer still has the flu. ‘Farmer.’ Theo’s birthday: huckleberry jam from her mother, for Theo — the Idaho gift. Next to his mother all night. ‘He’s *mine*. Since the beach cleanup.’ Toasted St. Martin de Porres: a dog and a cat and a mouse, one bowl. The Portolá steps, November 4th: her mom’s been calling me her boyfriend since September. She asked if she could tell her she’s right. I said yes. Her mom first, then Facebook. She flies home to Spokane the Wednesday before Thanksgiving. Her mother has named the turkey. She asked how I’m getting home. Greyhound. She frowned. Her mother sent a box: socks, cookies, two jars of huckleberry — JACK, and FOR THE CATHOLIC ROOMMATE. She offered me Daisy’s money. Six hundred and twelve dollars. It’s there, she says. Daisy doesn’t mind. Saturday, Ohio State in overtime: she gave me a photograph of the elephant seals in a frame she painted, every seal labeled with what it weighs. She’ll call during her dad’s grace on Thanksgiving so I can hear it. She wants to watch Michigan here, with me. ‘Someday I want to see your house. Is that okay to say?’

journal.title: Margot Lindqvist
journal.text: Margot Lindqvist. Has a folder on me. Called Lena and me useful idiots for Christian nationalism in front of four hundred people. Made a point about the Euthyphro I still can’t answer. Her mother teaches Classics at Reed. Held a wake for a cigarette on the roof and buried it at sea, for the prose. Had a brother. Her mother was forty-one; the test came back; they’d already picked the name. Anders. March 15, 2000. She’s defended her mother in every room since, and she defended her on the roof. Lena said his name. Doesn’t sleep. My friend. She has a faith column now, in the *Tide*, on a trial basis. If it’s boring they’ll kill it. She told me not to be boring. Came to Big Sur as an observer, for the monks — a functioning patriarchy in its natural habitat. Ran the *Tide*’s Ferrer follow-up from a minivan and wrote nothing down. Sunday at the coffee urn: ‘I’m not writing anything down.’ Halloween: Joan of Arc in duct tape, with her own haircut. Best Couple, with Pope Joan. She called it a category error and laughed anyway. Told me I’m surface acting. Hochschild, 1983. The flight attendants.

s18.slug: SATURDAY · 4:10 PM · DELGADO HALL, EAST STAIRWELL, 4TH-FLOOR LANDING
body: The RAZR goes off in his pocket before he’s up off the lounge carpet, and the little outside screen says DAD.
His father hasn’t called him since September. Jack takes it out to the east stairwell, to the third step up, and sits.

body.text: He was going to call at the final. Lena told him to — talk about the game, not the other thing. His father has beaten him to it.

body: “Overtime,” says Frank Costigan, from twenty-four hundred miles off. Behind him a space heater ticks and a radio is turned down low, and Jack could draw the garage from here: the Stroh’s fridge, the folding chair, the pegboard with the outlines of the tools on it.

choices.key: Your father called about Ohio State — the first time since September. You talked football: the Rose Bowl.
response: “Rose Bowl, Pop.”

“Pasadena,” his father says, like it’s a town he means to drive to. And then four minutes of it: the walk-on kicker who used to play soccer for money (Frank has decided not to hold it against him); Pryor’s legs, and what Frank would do about Pryor’s arm; the freshman from Iowa who should’ve been scared and wasn’t; Tressel’s play-calling in the third quarter, a matter Frank intends to take up with God. Jack says *yeah* and *I know* and *he did*. The heater ticks. Then: “Your mother says you needed money.”

response.text: “I got it,” Jack says. “Good,” says his father, and doesn’t ask how.
“My roommate spotted me.” “Pay him back.” “I will.”
“I got a second job. Nights. The library.” “Don’t waste it.”

response: “Go Bucks,” his father says, and the line clicks.

journal.title: Dad
journal.text: Frank Costigan. Twenty-six years on the line at Lordstown, laid off since June. Drove me 2,400 miles because two plane tickets cost more than the truck is worth. Saw the Pacific for the first time today. Didn’t say anything. That’s how you know. Monday the 9th: the SUB pay’s done. He went to the bar for the Steelers and didn’t come home. Sat in the employee lot at Lordstown to see if the lights were on. Hit the trash can pulling in at ten to five. Ma called me at one. Nobody was hurt. Saturday he called about Ohio State. Overtime. Pasadena. First time since September.

choices.key: Your father called about Ohio State. You told him Ma told you about Monday. “We don’t. Not here.”
response: “Ma told me about Monday.”
On the line there’s the garage — the heater, the radio, a car going by on Glenwood — and no father in it for a while.
“We don’t,” Frank says. “Not here.” The heater ticks. “That’s done.” Jack hears the folding chair take his weight differently. “Your mother says you needed money.”

s19.slug: SUNDAY · 12:50 AM · THE ANCHOR, THE END OF THE COUNTER
body: Ten to one and the end of the Saturday shift. The jukebox is dark, and the pie case is down to one wedge of lemon meringue sitting in its own light. Jack is on the last stool with his apron balled in his lap and his hands still pink from the sink.

body.text: Back in the kitchen, before he came out, Rudy watched him fold his tip-out into the Folgers can. The bills went in without a sound; there wasn’t much in there for them to land on. Rudy went back to wrapping the line and said nothing, for long enough that Jack heard it.

body: Gloria doesn’t come down the counter. She passes behind the server station with a bus tub on her hip, sets a coffee at his elbow across the gap without breaking stride, and keeps going to the urn, and with her back to him she asks, “How’s the pecan, hon?”
“She’s seeing somebody,” Jack says. “He’s nice.”
Gloria fills the urn to the line and screws the lid down. One breath.
“Lattice-top,” she says, and carries the bus tub through to Rudy.

journal.title: Gloria (the Anchor)
journal.text: Hired me for rating her pie a four. Rated me a lattice-top. I’m not going to ask. Told her I won’t be the next guy at the door. She says nobody holds a door that long without somebody else walking through it. Asked after the pecan. I said she’s seeing somebody, he’s nice. She said lattice-top.

body: At a quarter past eleven Sully’s bell hangs quiet, its rope tied off to the cleat. The Saints are in a dome in St. Louis against a team with one win, and it’s closer than it has any business being. Dale is on his stool at the end of the bar in the Barry Sanders jersey. Lena has the chair under the bell in her black and gold, one boot hooked on the rung and one hand on the cleat, like she’s minding a horse.

Becca came straight from the six o’clock touch tank and has already done the cow holler twice, on a field goal and on a first down, to general approval. Kevin drove; he sits at the end of the table, quiet, and watches the game like a chart. At ten Laney ordered a mimosa on the strength of a Louisiana driver’s license that says she’s twenty-four and named Mary Catherine Thibodeaux.

At the half Becca tows Jack to the Bloody Mary bar at the far end of the room for a virgin one, because of the celery. Up there the halftime show is a wall of noise — three men in suits shouting about tonight’s Colts game — and the table is a long way off. She leans in, practical and low. “Did you ask her yet?”

The second half kicks off before he can answer. Courtney Roby takes it at his own three and doesn’t stop, and the room comes up out of its chairs, and the line breaks, and Becca is swept off toward the table with both arms in the air, calling back over her shoulder, “I’m *praying*!”

Ninety-seven yards. The owner unties the rope, and Lena rings it for Roby standing up on the chair rung. Jack, back in the booth, gives the return a homily: a man with no kickoff touchdowns in his career, not one, and on the ninth Sunday the Lord says *go*. “It was Thomist, is what it was. He didn’t run toward the end zone. He ran away from everything that wasn’t the end zone.” Lena cracks up so hard she has to grab the rope to stay on the chair.

It’s a day when Brees throws two to the wrong team, and the Rams hang around. Then, early in the fourth, with the Rams within four, Brees finds Meachem from twenty-seven yards out, and the ball is in the air, and Sully’s is on its feet.

response: Jack is up on the booth seat before Meachem comes down with it. *WHO DAT* — from the bottom of a pair of Youngstown lungs — and Sully’s comes in under him, a hundred people in black and gold. Lena rings the bell for him, leaning back on the rope with all her weight, and when it’s over she reaches across and puts the end of it in his hand. It’s heavier than it looks, rough with a lot of Sundays, warm from her fist. Across the table Theo watches all of it and doesn’t clap.

It ends twenty-eight to twenty-three. Nine and oh. The owner unties the rope himself and rings it once more for the final. At Laney’s elbow the mimosa is still full to the brim, warm now, the orange gone pale at the top.

response.text: Out in the lot Kevin’s Odyssey has the WHO DAT on its back glass in La Vang polish, and Jack’s leaning 8 under it. Lena wipes the 8 off with her sleeve and holds out her hand to Kevin for the polish. “I’m not letting you near a nine,” she tells Jack, and does it herself, big and straight, and steps back to look.
response.else: Out in the lot Kevin’s Odyssey has the WHO DAT on its back glass in La Vang polish. Lena wipes off the 8 with her sleeve and holds out her hand to Kevin for the polish. “I’m not letting either of y’all near a nine,” she says, and does it herself, big and straight, and steps back to look.

response: “Becca,” Jack says, and points at her.

She’s on her feet with her celery. *WHO DAT* — half a second ahead of the room, in the voice she uses to call cattle off a county road, and meaning every letter of it — and the bar comes in behind her and loves her for it. Dale swivels clear round on his stool to see who that was. Lena rings the bell for her.

s25.slug: TUESDAY · 12:05 PM · PORTOLÁ HALL, THE FRONT STEPS
body: Becca has been on the Portolá steps since five to twelve, in the sun, with two coffees in a cardboard tray, a maple bar on a napkin on her knee, and an envelope in her lap, address side down, that she is very visibly not looking at.

body.text: “I got your text,” she says, before hello, and hands him his coffee. “I’m so sorry about Thanksgiving. I mean I’m *happy* for Lena, I am, but you wanted to —” She stops, and draws a zipper across her lips, firmly. It isn’t hers to say. She tears the maple bar in half and gives him the bigger half. “Julian’s so *nice*,” she says instead. “Lena should date somebody nice.”

“Mrs. Fitch says Lena brought her young man to the nine o’clock!” Becca hands him his coffee. “I thought he was just *coming*. The way Theo comes to Sully’s. But Mrs. Fitch says he held her coat for her, and in 1962 that meant something.” She tears the maple bar in half. “Julian’s so *nice*. Lena should date somebody nice.” Then she stops, with her half in her hand, and he can watch her do it — the nine o’clock, the coat, *not yet* at eleven o’clock that night — adding it up the way she’d add a feed bill, carrying the one. “You said not yet,” she says. There’s no edge on it anywhere. Then, before he can answer: “It’s okay. You don’t have to.” And she turns the envelope over in her lap.

“Mrs. Fitch says Lena brought her young man to the nine o’clock!” Becca hands him his coffee. “I thought he was just *coming*. The way Theo comes to Sully’s. But Mrs. Fitch says he held her coat for her, and in 1962 that meant something.” She tears the maple bar in half and gives him the bigger half. “Julian’s so *nice*. Lena should date somebody nice.” Then it reaches her. “Oh — so it’s just you on the bus.” She turns the envelope over in her lap. “*Unless*.”

body: The envelope is St. Brigid’s, the parish crest in the corner, his mother’s school-office hand on the front — the one on every permission slip at St. Brigid’s since before he was born. MISS REBECCA LINDELL, PORTOLÁ HALL. Inside, one sheet of the good notepaper.

body.title: St. Brigid of Kildare Parish · Youngstown, Ohio
body.text: …We would love to have you for a few days after Christmas, Rebecca, if your mother can spare you. Jack’s grandmother would like to meet the girl who writes on cows. With love, Maria Costigan

body: Her mother said yes before Becca finished the sentence; her father said “*Pittsburgh?*” the way he says *coyote*, and then yes. December twenty-seventh to the thirtieth. She has the flights printed already, Spokane to Pittsburgh through Denver — “it’s closer than Cleveland, I *looked*” — and the planner is open on the step beside her to a page headed OHIO!! with a list down it in green. ROSIE — crab book. NONNA — ??? GINA — ??? The crab book is half done, the pages tucked in the back of the planner: Thomas the hermit crab, drawn in marker, one page per true fact, the chip in his shell on every page so Rosie will know it’s him. “Is Youngstown a coat place or a coat-and-boots place? I have the boots. I have *so* many boots.”
“What does Nonna like? Is it bad I’ve never seen snow that wasn’t *ours*?” She looks at him with the whole sun on her face. “Jack. Your *house*.”

response: “They’ll love you,” Jack says, and it’s true.
Becca uncaps the green pen and writes, on her own, NONNA — ROSARY? and underlines the question mark twice.
Then she taps the letter twice against his chest, like a ticket being punched, and takes her coffee up the steps to her one o’clock with the planner under her arm.
“Let me talk to Ma.”
“Of course! She said you’d say that.” Becca finds the line for him, halfway down the first side, where his mother has written *He’ll want to talk to me first. Let him.* “See? She knows you.”
Then she taps the letter twice against his chest, like a ticket being punched, and takes her coffee up the steps to her one o’clock with the planner under her arm.

choices.text: Hold the planner while she pencils PIT? on the twenty-seventh. Say nothing.
response: She hands him the planner open to December, and he holds it flat on his palm while she finds the pencil behind her ear and writes PIT? in the box for the twenty-seventh, small and neat, and BACK? on the thirtieth, and blows the eraser crumbs off his hand. He doesn’t say anything. She takes it back and closes it on the pencil.
Then she taps the letter twice against his chest, like a ticket being punched, and takes her coffee up the steps to her one o’clock with the planner under her arm.

journal.title: Becca Lindell
journal.text: Coeur d’Alene. Seven siblings; wants seven or nine kids, odd numbers, for the tiebreaker. Can butcher a deer — elk too. Has pulled a calf, and it shows. Ran the beach cleanup like a cattle drive and put me on her team. Asked about the scar in the water. Told her mother the cleanup was a date, then asked me if it was. Wrote FRIDAY? on her clipboard, and meant it. Drives her brother Eli’s red Ranger; St. Isidore on the visor. Second date: Friday-night football. Knows downs. Prayed a Glory Be on fourth and one. Learned the First Way on the bleachers and said it back perfectly. Kissed my cheek so there’s no confusion. Third date was mine. I asked. I paid. The elephant seals at Piedras Blancas at sunset, in Kevin’s Odyssey. She knew what every one of them weighed. Nobody’s ever planned a thing for her, she says. She’s been praying for two in the morning. Named a hermit crab Thomas, after the First Way, and asked Fr. Osei whose blessing it was. Works the Marine Lab touch tank Thursday afternoons and Friday at six in the morning — that’s how she signed Thomas out. He’s home; she knows him by the chip in his shell. Mailed Rosie a birthday card with Thomas on it and six true facts on the back, to the address I gave her for her Christmas cards. She does them in October. Has a page on her clipboard for Wes. She’s been praying for him and Lena since September. Her eyes are gray. Brought a survival bag to the library for my midterm, with a clementine for Lena. Prays at two, like always. Took me to *Where the Wild Things Are* at the Rialto; her favorite line is the last one. My mother wrote her a thank-you note. Her list for Halloween says WE SHOULD MATCH!! It’s due Halloween. She says I look at her like homework. She says she’ll wait. Stuck on the touch tank all weekend while we were at Big Sur: the weekend volunteer has the swine flu. Asked me for the monks’ fruitcake for her Grandma Agnes — the only honest fruitcake in America. I handed in my homework six days early. St. Isidore and St. Maria: her first. Early, she said. Nobody’s early but her. Halloween: she sewed my costume out of a Rathdrum Feed & Seed sack. She was St. Maria de la Cabeza in Mrs. Fitch’s lace, with a water jug. Best Saint, by acclamation — a gold halo. Never won anything that wasn’t a heifer. Home at 11:40 for the six o’clock tank; the volunteer still has the flu. ‘Farmer.’ Theo’s birthday: huckleberry jam from her mother, for Theo — the Idaho gift. Next to his mother all night. ‘He’s *mine*. Since the beach cleanup.’ Toasted St. Martin de Porres: a dog and a cat and a mouse, one bowl. The Portolá steps, November 4th: her mom’s been calling me her boyfriend since September. She asked if she could tell her she’s right. I said yes. Her mom first, then Facebook. She flies home to Spokane the Wednesday before Thanksgiving. Her mother has named the turkey. She asked how I’m getting home. Greyhound. She frowned. Her mother sent a box: socks, cookies, two jars of huckleberry — JACK, and FOR THE CATHOLIC ROOMMATE. She offered me Daisy’s money. Six hundred and twelve dollars. It’s there, she says. Daisy doesn’t mind. Saturday, Ohio State in overtime: she gave me a photograph of the elephant seals in a frame she painted, every seal labeled with what it weighs. She’ll call during her dad’s grace on Thanksgiving so I can hear it. She wants to watch Michigan here, with me. ‘Someday I want to see your house. Is that okay to say?’ Ma wrote her. Three days after Christmas. Pittsburgh’s closer than Cleveland. She looked.

Theo is at his desk under the lamp with a screenplay he would never call a screenplay, and he looks up when the door opens, and keeps looking. “Costigan?”
“I ended it.”

Theo closes the screenplay. He doesn’t say one clever thing. He gets up and takes his jar down off the shelf by the espresso machine — FOR THE CATHOLIC ROOMMATE, in Mrs. Lindell’s Sharpie — and works the lid until the seal gives with a small gasp, and gets two spoons out of the drawer where he keeps the good spoons, and hands Jack one.

They sit on Theo’s bed with their backs against the wall and eat huckleberry jam out of the jar. It’s sweet and sharp and tastes like somewhere colder than here. Jack is four spoonfuls in before he notices he’s eating.

body.text: “My calendar says I’m supposed to ask you something after Thanksgiving,” Theo says. “I’m going to let it.”

body: His iPhone lights up on the desk. He reaches over and types on it with his thumbs, quick, and sets it face down again; Jack sees the light go across the ceiling and none of the words.

body.text: Then Theo takes the Residential Services receipt out of his desk drawer, turns it over, and under $340.00 and + 1 PIE (PEACH) writes, in small square capitals: + 1 JAR (HUCKLEBERRY). FORGIVEN.

response: At twenty to eight Jack stands his spoon up in the jar and gets his jacket. Theo takes custody of the jar. “Go,” he says. “I’ll guard the jam.”
Jack keeps his back to the wall and his spoon in his hand.

s29a.slug: WEDNESDAY · 8:00 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE CONFESSIONAL
body: The confessional at St. Brendan’s was a coat closet once, and there are still hooks above the kneeler. KNOCK (gently), says the card on the door. A low lamp burns on the far side of the linen screen, and behind it Fr. Osei breathes slow and waits. Twice in eleven days; the screen doesn’t keep count, and neither does the man behind it.
It isn’t the breakup Jack confesses. He did that honest, or as honest as he had in him, in a truck with the heater running. It’s the six weeks before.

“I let her love me so I wouldn’t have to decide anything,” he says. “She kept showing up with things. Jam. A frame she painted. A whole plan. And I took it, and I let her think I was taking it the way she was giving it. I let her plan Christmas. I let my mother write her a letter. I knew the entire time, Father. I just didn’t say it out loud, even to me.”

The lamp hums. Fr. Osei is quiet. “My grandmother used to say the one who is carried on the back does not know how far the town is,” he says. “She carried you six weeks. Now you know the distance. Good. That is where your sorrow starts, my friend. Not where it ends.”
He gives the absolution in English, unhurried, and then the penance. “Pray for her by name, every day, until Advent. Don’t skip the name.”

Out in the courtyard the olive tree is a black shape against no moon, and the broken sprinkler stands up out of the dry grass. Jack stands by the wall and says her name once, out loud, so it’s been said somewhere. “Becca.”

Theo puts on something black and white and French — a man in a raincoat on a bridge — sets the laptop on the desk where they can both see it, and doesn’t press play. The first frame sits there with the subtitles waiting to be needed.
Two spoons in the jar. Theo takes his turn, then Jack. The jam goes down a finger. Somebody on the Lagoon path laughs at something and is gone.
Theo lies back on his pillow with his spoon. To the ceiling: “She’s a wonderful girl.”
Jack passes him the jar.

s31.slug: THURSDAY · 12:02 AM · EAST STAIRWELL → THE 2ND-FLOOR HALL
body: Jack carries Lena’s mug down the east stairs to the second floor, to the kitchenette by the elevator, and pours the coffee out — gone flat and dark, with a skin on it — and rinses the mug under the hot tap until the ring comes off, and dries it on his shirt. COMMUNITY COFFEE, it says, in red, from Louisiana.

217’s door is open about four inches. Light from inside lies across the hall carpet in a stripe. Laney is standing in the gap in her PI LAM LITTLE shirt, one hand on the frame, looking back into the room at something Jack can’t see from where he is.
She turns her head and sees him. Jack doesn’t have a word for what her face is doing. Her eyes go to the mug in his hand, and back to him.
Then she closes the door, softly, all the way, without a word.
Jack stands in the hall a minute. He sets the clean mug down on the carpet beside the door, the handle turned out so whoever opens it in the morning won’t kick it over.
412 is dark. Theo is sitting up in bed with his iPhone at his ear, leaving a message on a machine at twenty-five past midnight in his brightest voice.
“Harbor Inn? Vance. Two, Saturday at eight, under Costigan. C-O-S-T-I-G-A-N. A window, if you have one, the one by the piano if you have that. Thank you *so* much.”
He hangs up and finds Jack looking at him from the other bed.
“My mother’s coming up,” Theo says. “She wants to meet Gloria.”

He plugs the phone in and lies down, and the screen goes dark on the nightstand. On the floor between the beds the jam jar stands with two spoons in it. On Jack’s desk, by the window, Becca’s frame catches a little of the sodium light from the lawn: the two of them in the middle of it, and the painted seals going round the frame, every one of them holding on to what it weighs.
